nameStory: The name "baby's-breath" comes from the plant's cloud-like masses of tiny, delicate white flowers that seem as light and airy as a baby's gentle breathing. The "glandular" part refers to the small, sticky glands you can feel on the stems and leaves that help distinguish this species from its more common cousins.
description: Glandular baby's-breath is a delicate annual wildflower that creates airy sprays of tiny white flowers on branching stems. Growing 1-3 feet tall, this member of the pink family has narrow, grass-like leaves and a loose, open growth habit. Unlike the fluffy baby's-breath you might see in flower arrangements, this wild species has a more sparse, wiry appearance with sticky-feeling stems.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny white flowers less than 1/4 inch across with 5 petals, arranged in loose, branching clusters that create an open, airy appearance

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Feel sticky or tacky to the touch due to tiny glands - run your finger along the stem and you'll notice it's not smooth like other baby's-breaths

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Narrow, linear leaves that feel somewhat thick and fleshy, arranged opposite each other on the stem, often with a bluish-green tint

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Branching annual that grows 1-3 feet tall with a loose, open structure that sways easily in the breeze

idTips.label: Seeds
idTips.description: Small, dark seeds contained in papery capsules that split open when ripe, often persistent into fall

habitat: This rare species is typically found in disturbed soils, roadsides, and waste areas, often in sandy or gravelly locations. In New England, it's most likely to appear in areas with calcium-rich soils or near limestone outcrops. With only 3 recorded observations in the region, it's an uncommon find that may be associated with areas of human disturbance or construction sites.

seasonality.spring: Young plants emerge as small rosettes of narrow leaves, beginning their branching growth as weather warms.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming season from June through August, when the characteristic tiny white flowers create their airy display and sticky stems are most noticeable.
seasonality.fall: Flowers fade and seed capsules develop, turning brown and papery while often remaining attached to the dried stems.
seasonality.winter: Annual plants die back completely, leaving only seeds to germinate the following spring.

funFact: The sticky glands that give this plant its name actually serve as tiny insect traps - small gnats and other tiny bugs can get stuck to the stems, providing the plant with extra nutrients like a miniature version of a carnivorous plant!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with the common baby's-breath (Gypsophila paniculata) found in gardens and floral arrangements, but that species has smooth, non-sticky stems and grows much larger. Remember: if it feels sticky, you've found the glandular species!
contextualKnowledge: While baby's-breath is beloved by florists for its delicate appearance, the glandular species is actually quite rare in New England and may represent scattered introductions rather than established populations. Don't expect to find this in every field - it's a genuine botanical treasure when encountered.
compareHints: Unlike common baby's-breath which has smooth stems and grows into large perennial clumps, glandular baby's-breath is an annual with distinctly sticky, glandular stems. It's smaller and more delicate than showy baby's-breath, and unlike cowherb, it has narrow leaves rather than broad, clasping ones.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among its Gypsophila relatives in New England, cowherb is unique for its blue-gray waxy appearance and pale pink flowers.
Showy baby's-breath differs from regular baby's-breath by being an annual (lives one season) rather than perennial, and having larger, showier individual flowers.
Baby's-breath differs from its relatives like cowherb by forming much larger, bushier plants with more extensively branched flower clusters.
